task.goal: Help a two-person household waste less fresh food when work schedules change unpredictably.
hard_constraints: No new appliance, food tracking app or assumption of daily shopping.
Respect food safety dates and do not recommend eating spoiled food.
Compare discarded food, meal flexibility and planning time over three weeks.
task.available_resources: Existing fridge, freezer and paper notes.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep fresh commitments small; freeze the uncertain portion
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is to limit how much food depends on both people being home soon. At the household’s usual shopping interval, buy fresh food for only the meals reasonably likely to happen before it needs using. Cover uncertain meals with existing freezer portions and longer-lasting foods. This does not require more frequent shopping.

After shopping, divide suitable perishables into two-person or single-person portions. Keep only the near-term amount refrigerated; freeze the rest promptly while safe, following package instructions. Label frozen portions with contents and freezing date, retaining any relevant preparation instructions. Avoid freezing items already beyond their safety date. Thaw and cook according to safe handling guidance; freezing does not rescue spoiled food or reset an expired safety date.

Use one paper note listing refrigerated meal portions and available freezer meals. When schedules change, leave frozen portions frozen. When one person is home, use a single portion. Check the note before the usual shopping trip so replacements reflect actual consumption.

This could work because a cancelled dinner stops creating an urgent obligation to eat fresh ingredients. It assumes usable freezer space, suitable foods and willingness to portion purchases. Limits include freezer crowding, texture changes and meals that require advance thawing. Start with just one commonly wasted ingredient rather than reorganizing everything.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For three weeks, record discarded edible food in consistent units such as portions, why it was discarded, meals that accommodated a schedule change without an extra shop, and minutes spent planning, labeling and portioning. Use the household’s ordinary routine in week one as the simple comparator; use this routine in weeks two and three. Record meals eaten at home and schedule disruptions to help interpret differences. At the end, inspect remaining frozen portions so accumulating stock is not mistaken for proven waste reduction. The mechanism is challenged if refrigerator discards do not decline, freezing merely shifts waste into storage, or preparation time and thawing constraints make changed schedules harder to handle. Three weeks provides a practical signal, not a reliable long-term estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use interchangeable ingredients instead of assigning dinners to days
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is ingredient substitutability: buy a small set of fresh ingredients that can serve several meals, rather than ingredients committed to particular recipes or dates. A cancelled meal then leaves useful components instead of an incomplete recipe kit.

Before the normal shopping trip, choose two or three meal formats the household already likes, such as a bowl, a wrap and a soup. Pick overlapping ingredients that can safely fit several formats. On paper, write a short ingredient-to-meal map, including approximate single-person and two-person quantities. Buy quantities matched to plausible meals at home, and choose a mixture of shorter- and longer-lasting ingredients. Use existing frozen food to fill gaps where available.

At dinner, whoever is home chooses a format around the ingredient that needs using first. Cook only the required quantity where practical. Keep ingredients separate until serving when doing so preserves their usefulness. Follow storage instructions and safety dates for each component; cooking or combining ingredients must not be used to extend an unsafe item’s life. Freeze suitable surplus promptly if plans collapse.

This could work by reducing the number of ingredients stranded when a particular dinner disappears. It requires some overlap in food preferences and a few familiar, adaptable dishes. It can fail when diets differ substantially, when every format depends on the same missing ingredient, or when repetition becomes unwelcome. Implementation needs only a paper map and existing storage; elaborate batch cooking is unnecessary.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over three weeks, compare ordinary recipe-by-day planning in week one with interchangeable ingredients in weeks two and three. Record discarded edible food by portions or another consistent measure, changed-schedule meals assembled without an extra shop, and total planning and dinner-decision minutes. Note meals at home and disruptions. For a small direct check, take one actual cancelled dinner and inspect whether its remaining ingredients can make an acceptable meal for whoever is home, within their available time. Count failures as well as successes. The proposal is weakened if ingredients still become stranded, acceptable choices shrink, or reduced waste requires substantially more decision time. Different weekly schedules and purchases limit causal conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make urgent food visible and assign the next action
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is a shared handoff: turn approaching food deadlines into visible, assigned actions so neither person assumes the other will use an item. This targets household coordination rather than changing the meal repertoire or relying primarily on freezing purchases.

Designate a clearly visible refrigerator area for food needing attention, without violating safe storage separation or temperature requirements. Keep raw foods contained and appropriately positioned. Put a paper note nearby with no more than a few entries: item, relevant safety deadline or storage guidance, next action, and the person taking responsibility. Actions might be “use in lunch,” “cook tonight,” or “freeze today if suitable.” Preserve original labels; the note must not replace or extend package safety instructions.

Review the note together before the normal shopping trip and twice between trips. If a work change cancels an assigned use, the responsible person updates the paper at the next opportunity and selects a feasible alternative. Each person can check the note when arriving home. Remove completed entries and avoid cataloguing every food item. An item whose safe handling history is uncertain should not be treated as safe merely because it appears on the list.

This could work because attention and responsibility persist when dinner plans change. It assumes both people can access and maintain the note and usually have enough notice to act before deadlines. It cannot solve prolonged absences or consistently excessive purchasing by itself. The implementation requires a small fridge area, paper and brief scheduled reviews; excessive bookkeeping would undermine it.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the ordinary routine in week one, then the visible handoff routine in weeks two and three. Record discarded edible food consistently, successful meal changes without an extra shop, and all planning and note-maintenance minutes. Record meals at home and work disruptions. For each discarded item, check whether it was absent from the note, assigned too late, or assigned but not acted on. A small falsifying check is whether an actual cancelled meal produces a clear, timely replacement action that either person can identify from the paper. If listed food is discarded as often as before, assignments repeatedly go stale, or maintenance exceeds the household’s acceptable effort, visibility is probably not the main missing mechanism. Three weeks may expose coordination failures but cannot establish durable habit formation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Move fresh-food use to the meals that actually happen
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is to redirect fresh food from unreliable shared dinners into breakfast, lunch or separate meals that each person already eats. A cancelled dinner then loses its calendar slot without necessarily losing the opportunity to use its ingredients. This changes when and where household food is consumed.

Before the usual shopping trip, identify a few existing meal occasions that tend to survive work changes. Each person chooses one familiar way to use household perishables at those occasions: vegetables with breakfast eggs, fruit alongside breakfast, or suitable dinner ingredients in a packed lunch. On paper, write these fallback uses beside the fresh foods purchased. Keep quantities within normal appetite; the aim is to replace another meal or ingredient, not add eating occasions.

When a shared dinner falls through, redirect its ingredients to the next feasible existing meal. Prepare only what that person will eat. If neither person has a suitable opportunity before an item's safety deadline, this routine has reached its limit; follow safe storage or disposal guidance rather than treating the fallback plan as permission to keep it longer.

Implementation uses the existing fridge and a short paper list. Packed meals require existing suitable containers and safe refrigeration or temperature control; otherwise restrict fallback uses to meals at home. Respect package dates, storage instructions and safe handling throughout.

This could work if dinners are substantially less predictable than other meals and both people accept some ingredients outside dinner. It will help less if work disrupts every meal, workplace storage is unavailable, or redirected meals simply create surplus elsewhere. Shopping should account for the foods these substitutions displace.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Compare the ordinary routine in week one with meal redirection in weeks two and three. Record discarded food in consistent portions, meals successfully adapted after schedule changes, failed adaptations, and planning minutes, including fallback preparation decisions. Note meals at home, disruptions and any purchased meals replaced.

For the smallest falsifying check, follow the ingredients from one cancelled dinner: were they safely eaten at an existing meal before their deadlines, and did their substitutes subsequently go unused? Inspect remaining fresh stock at each week's end. The mechanism is weakened if food merely changes its planned destination, waste shifts to displaced ingredients, or flexibility requires unacceptable effort. Three unequal weeks provide a practical comparison, not strong causal evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Preserve useful life by delaying opening and preparation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is to reduce avoidable deterioration before food is needed. Opening several packages or washing, cutting and mixing ingredients for anticipated dinners can make cancelled meals more costly. Keeping food in its appropriate unopened or whole state preserves options when work schedules change.

At the normal shopping interval, identify two commonly discarded foods whose storage instructions distinguish unopened from opened storage, or whose quality suffers after preparation. Use a simple rule: finish an existing open package before opening another equivalent one, and prepare only the amount needed for the meal actually happening. Keep remaining ingredients separate and appropriately stored. Do not postpone preparation when the manufacturer's instructions require immediate action.

Use existing packaging and suitable containers already available. Follow food-specific storage guidance, keep refrigerator airflow clear, and separate raw food safely from ready-to-eat food. On paper, record opening dates and any instruction such as “use within three days of opening.” Follow whichever applicable safety deadline comes first; an unopened package is not permission to exceed its use-by date. Discard spoiled food, and do not rely on appearance or smell to establish safety.

This could work when waste comes from premature preparation, duplicate open packages or inappropriate storage. It requires foods that benefit from remaining unopened or unprepared, adequate existing storage, and willingness to do some preparation at mealtime. It may offer little benefit if purchases already exceed consumption or prolonged absences outlast safe storage. Delayed preparation can also make a rushed dinner less convenient.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Compare the ordinary routine in week one with this routine in weeks two and three, keeping the usual shopping frequency. Record discarded food in consistent portions, successful and failed meal adaptations after schedule changes, and planning minutes. Record preparation minutes separately to expose any transferred effort, plus meals at home and disruptions.

The smallest check follows one frequently wasted food through a cancelled dinner: does leaving it unopened or unprepared preserve a safe, practical later use? Inspect remaining stock at each week's end. If discards persist, merely occur later, or extra preparation prevents flexible meals, the mechanism is weakened. Three weeks gives a preliminary comparison; unequal schedules limit attribution.

EXPAND.title: Give fresh food a second destination: lunches
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to move some fresh-food consumption away from unpredictable shared dinners. Ingredients purchased for dinner also have an agreed route into breakfasts or packed lunches, so a cancelled evening meal need not cancel their use altogether. This changes when food gets eaten, rather than primarily changing storage or assigning responsibility.

At the usual shopping interval, identify one or two commonly wasted foods that both people already enjoy at another meal. Write a short fallback on paper: for example, tomatoes with breakfast or vegetables in a familiar lunch. Use existing ingredients and containers; do not buy additional fresh food specifically for the fallback. When dinner is cancelled, either person can use the affected food at their next suitable meal, replacing something they would otherwise eat.

Keep the routine small: one fallback per selected food and a quick decision when plans change. Follow package dates, refrigeration requirements and safe handling guidance. Packed perishables require suitable cold storage during transport and at work. If that is unavailable, use the fallback at home instead.

This could work because work changes may remove shared dinners while leaving other eating opportunities intact. It assumes at least one person has reasonably dependable breakfasts or lunches, suitable food preferences and time to assemble them. Existing containers and safe storage are prerequisites for packed meals. It will offer little protection if work disrupts every meal, food remains inaccessible at home, or the fallback simply causes a different perishable food to be wasted.
EXPAND.experiment: Use the ordinary routine in week one and the fallback routine in weeks two and three. On paper, record discarded food in consistent portions, meals at home, schedule disruptions, changed meals accommodated without an extra shop, and planning minutes including fallback decisions. Include any displaced lunch ingredients in discard totals. For the smallest check, follow one actual cancelled dinner: does its fresh food replace another meal before its safety deadline? The mechanism is weakened if food merely moves between meal plans without being eaten, flexibility declines, or planning time rises beyond the household’s acceptable effort. Three uneven weeks provide an initial comparison, not proof of lasting savings.

EXPAND.title: Choose fresh foods with a longer usable window
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to slow deterioration through purchasing form and correct storage. At the same shopping frequency and broadly similar quantities, replace a few frequently wasted, fragile items with acceptable fresh alternatives that usually tolerate a longer wait. This buys time when work postpones cooking.

Before the usual shop, identify two recurring losses. Possible substitutions include whole carrots for a prepared salad mix or a whole cabbage for delicate leaves, where these fit meals the household already likes. These are examples, not guarantees: condition at purchase, package instructions and actual storage matter. Keep quantities comparable so the trial tests a longer usable window rather than simply buying less.

Write the substitutions and their intended storage on a paper note. Use existing fridge compartments appropriately, keep foods requiring refrigeration cold, and avoid unnecessary cutting or washing before storage when guidance recommends keeping them whole and dry. Preserve labels and follow safety dates. Longer expected quality does not override a use-by date, and smell or appearance cannot establish the safety of every food.

The routine needs no full inventory or elaborate meal map. Its main implementation work is selecting acceptable substitutes and checking their storage requirements once. It assumes the household can tolerate some ingredient changes and has suitable fridge space. Longer-lasting foods may require more preparation or may be less appealing, which can erase the benefit. This approach is also less useful when losses are mainly short-dated animal products or prepared meals without an acceptable substitute.
EXPAND.experiment: In week one, record the usual foods; in weeks two and three, make the selected substitutions. Compare discarded portions, successful meals after schedule changes without an extra shop, and planning minutes, including time spent choosing substitutes. Note preparation effort separately because extra chopping could make meals less feasible. Record meals eaten at home and disruptions. The smallest check is whether one substituted food remains safely usable and desirable through an actual delay that previously stranded its counterpart. Reject the substitution if it is still discarded, demands unavailable cooking time, or reduces acceptable meal choices. Inspect remaining stock at the end: unconsumed durable food is not yet demonstrated waste prevention. Differences in shopping quality and weekly schedules limit the comparison.

EXPAND.title: Arrange a small surplus-sharing outlet
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to transfer usable food to another household when this household no longer has a realistic opportunity to eat it. Work disruption can reduce demand abruptly; a willing nearby recipient supplies another opportunity for consumption. This is most useful for occasional surplus that cannot conveniently be incorporated into another meal.

Before relying on the routine, establish whether one existing friend, relative or neighbour actually wants occasional offers and can collect or receive food conveniently. Participation must be voluntary, with no expectation of reciprocity. If no suitable person exists, this alternative is not usable.

When a schedule change leaves surplus, first check whether the household still expects to use it safely. If not, offer a small, specific amount while it has sufficient safe life remaining. Prefer whole produce or unopened, correctly stored products for a simple trial. Keep original packaging and communicate relevant dates, ingredients and storage history. Do not transfer food with uncertain handling, compromised packaging or signs of spoilage. Perishables must remain safely chilled through handover; sharing does not extend their safety dates.

Use a paper note to record what left, when and whether the recipient later confirms using it. Ordinary communication and an existing nearby relationship are prerequisites beyond the listed storage resources. Avoid special trips or buying extra with sharing in mind. The main limits are recipient availability, transport, dietary compatibility and the possibility of moving waste elsewhere. Sharing also gives up food that might otherwise have supported a later household meal, so preserve enough for realistic needs.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the ordinary routine in week one with sharing in weeks two and three. Record household discarded portions, portions transferred, confirmed recipient use where available, changed-schedule meals accommodated without an extra shop, and planning or coordination minutes. Note meals at home and disruptions. Keep transfers separate from confirmed consumption: a lower household bin total alone does not demonstrate less overall waste. The smallest falsifying check is one genuine surplus offer following a cancellation: can it reach a willing recipient safely and with little effort, and is it actually used? The mechanism is weakened if offers repeatedly fail, recipients discard the food, or sharing leaves the original household short of flexible meals. Three weeks may contain too few transfers for a confident judgment.

EXPAND.title: Move preparation to a reliable window so late arrivals can still eat at home
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is to separate preparation time from eating time. If fresh food is discarded because an unexpected late finish makes cooking feel impractical, doing the necessary work earlier can turn that food into an achievable dinner. This targets the effort required when someone arrives home tired.

Choose one familiar meal that both people enjoy and that safely tolerates advance preparation. At an already available window after the usual shopping trip, prepare only enough for the next realistically expected meals within its safe storage period. Depending on the dish, this could mean cooking a complete meal or preparing its most time-consuming component. Use existing cookware and covered food-safe containers; if suitable containers are unavailable, this alternative needs adjustment. Write the contents, preparation date, applicable storage deadline and reheating instructions on paper. Keep original ingredient labels where relevant.

Portion for independent arrivals so either person can finish or reheat their serving without waiting for the other. Choose something with little remaining work and cleanup. Follow applicable cooling, refrigeration and reheating guidance; advance preparation can shorten the usable window for some ingredients. Discard food when required by safety dates or handling history.

This assumes there is a reasonably dependable preparation window and that late-arrival cooking effort is a meaningful cause of waste. It uses the existing fridge, ordinary kitchen equipment and paper, without requiring additional shopping. It may increase total preparation time or disappoint people who dislike reheated food. It offers little benefit when both people are absent altogether, and preparing too much could increase waste.
EXPAND.experiment: Run a three-week comparison: ordinary preparation in week one, advance preparation in weeks two and three, keeping shopping frequency and intended portions broadly comparable. Each week, record discarded edible food in consistent household units, total planning minutes, and preparation minutes separately. Record schedule disruptions and whether each person could obtain a suitable meal from the purchased food despite them. Include waste from other foods displaced by the prepared meals. The mechanism is unsupported if disrupted evenings do not become easier to accommodate, discarded food stays level or rises, or the added preparation burden makes the routine unacceptable. Three weeks provides a practical household check, not strong causal evidence; unequal work disruptions can obscure the comparison.
